abstract_text: The Golgi apparatus is a highly organized mesoscale organelle characterized by its distinct architecture of stacked, flattened cisternae. This unique structural emergence is essential for the sequential processing and sorting of cellular cargo. Despite decades of morphological studies, the biophysical mechanisms by which dynamic membrane tethering and localized lipid sorting drive the self-organization of these stacks—and how this architecture dictates the emergent property of efficient secretory flux—remain fundamentally unresolved. Understanding this mesoscale phenomenon is crucial for explaining how cells manage massive intracellular transport networks. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent dynamics of Golgi stacking and secretory flux. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including spatial proteomics, high-resolution 3D electron microscopy, and lipidomics from repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas, EMPIAR, and the Metabolomics Workbench. By employing advanced topological data analysis and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic network of membrane interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local molecular tethering leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional Golgi architecture. The complexity of Golgi biophysics requires the integration of structural imaging with multi-omics data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites membrane traffic biologists, computational biophysicists, lipidomics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular transport networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale transport hubs, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.
main_idea: This research investigates the biophysical mechanisms governing Golgi apparatus self assembly to address the lack of quantitative models linking architecture. The study employs topological data analysis and physics informed graph neural networks to integrate disparate multi omics and structural datasets. This project establishes a unified predictive framework that reveals how mesoscale organization emerges from molecular components to regulate secretion.

title: Decoding the Emergent Assembly of Plant Cell Wall Cellulose Synthase Rosettes
title_norm: decoding the emergent assembly of plant cell wall cellulose synthase rosettes
standardized_text:
Plant cell biology and mechanobiology investigate how cellulose synthase (CESA) rosettes assemble and function within the plasma membrane. Current knowledge confirms that CESA rosettes synthesize cellulose microfibrils while moving along cortical microtubules despite unknown assembly mechanisms. This project decodes the biophysical rules of CESA rosette assembly to explain how nanoscale protein interactions produce functional matrices.

The study employs a community scale data synthesis project using artificial intelligence and machine learning to integrate existing datasets. Researchers apply graph neural networks for protein interaction modeling and convolutional neural networks for particle tracking of live cell imaging. Results are validated through a unified predictive model that maps molecular states to observed mesoscale behavioral phenotypes.

The project utilizes datasets from the Arabidopsis Information Resource, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE database, and Image Data Resource. Multi modal datasets are curated and standardized using machine learning algorithms to create a comprehensive multi scale predictive model. Potential inconsistencies in disparate datasets are mitigated through collaborative curation by a team of data scientists and biologists.

The proposal does not address the project timeline or specific milestones for the research. This project requires transdisciplinary expertise in plant biology, computational biophysics, proteomics, and data science to integrate complex data.

All synthesized datasets, artificial intelligence models, and codebases will be released publicly via Zenodo and GitHub. The team includes plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists across various career stages and institutions.

abstract_text: The plant cell wall is a massive, extracellular mesoscale matrix that dictates cellular shape, growth, and defense. The fundamental building blocks of this wall, cellulose microfibrils, are synthesized by highly organized, hexameric protein complexes known as cellulose synthase (CESA) rosettes. The dynamic assembly of these mesoscale rosettes at the plasma membrane and their collective movement driven by the underlying cytoskeleton represent a profound example of biological emergence. However, the precise rules governing how individual CESA proteins self-assemble and coordinate to produce highly ordered cellulose microfibrils remain a long-standing puzzle. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis project to unravel the emergent properties of CESA rosette assembly and function. We will integrate publicly available transcriptomics, proteomics, and high-resolution live-cell imaging datasets from repositories such as the Arabidopsis Information Resource, PRIDE, and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced graph neural networks and particle-tracking machine learning algorithms, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to model the dynamic spatio-temporal assembly of rosettes without generating new experimental data. This AI-driven synthesis will reveal the hidden biophysical rules that govern how nanoscale protein interactions scale up to produce mesoscale extracellular matrices. The integration of complex biomechanical data with plant multi-omics requires a level of transdisciplinary collaboration that can only be supported by NCEMS. Our working group brings together plant cell biologists, computational biophysicists, proteomics experts, and data scientists. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from varying career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity is essential for fostering the innovative analytical strategies required to tackle plant mechanobiological emergence. A major focus of our initiative is to train the next generation of researchers in data-intensive biology. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, machine learning, and collaborative software development. We are fully committed to gold-standard open science practices; all synthesized datasets, AI models, and codebases will be made publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing existing structural and molecular data, this project will answer long-standing questions about how plant cells process physical information, revealing the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.
main_idea: This research investigates the unknown biophysical rules governing how individual cellulose synthase proteins transition into functional hexameric rosettes within plants. The study employs graph neural networks and convolutional architectures to integrate disparate multi omics and imaging datasets into a unified framework. This project provides a novel predictive model that maps molecular protein interactions to the emergence of complex extracellular matrix structures.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Assembly of Bacterial Microcompartments
title_norm: synthesizing the emergent assembly of bacterial microcompartments
standardized_text:
This project investigates bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to determine the mechanisms of mesoscale proteinaceous organelle self assembly. Current knowledge includes siloed structural data and genomic sequences that prevent a systems level understanding of organelle assembly. The study decodes emergent assembly pathways to explain how weak protein interactions drive robust and deterministic mesoscale architecture.

The study design involves a three phase initiative consisting of data aggregation and AI driven structural synthesis and modeling. Key methods include AlphaFold Multimer for structural prediction and Graph Neural Networks for interactome analysis and reinforcement learning for simulations. Structural biologists will validate results by comparing predicted interaction interfaces and assembly pathways against existing empirical structural and proteomics data.

The project utilizes datasets from the NCBI and the Protein Data Bank and the PRIDE proteomics and interactomics repository. Automated pipelines will standardize metadata and resolve nomenclature to map genomic sequences to structural models in one database. Inconsistencies in nomenclature and metadata across repositories will be addressed through automated harmonization pipelines to mitigate known data limitations.

The proposal does not address the project timeline or specific milestones for the research. The project requires a transdisciplinary team of biologists and engineers to integrate disparate data types beyond one lab scope.

All findings and integrated databases and analytical workflows will be made publicly accessible via GitHub and community standard repositories. The team includes biologists and engineers across career stages with training opportunities for two postdoctoral researchers and three students.

abstract_text: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), such as carboxysomes, are highly sophisticated, mesoscale proteinaceous organelles that encapsulate specific metabolic pathways to enhance efficiency and prevent the release of toxic intermediates. The self-assembly of thousands of shell proteins and internal enzymes into a geometrically precise, functional polyhedral structure is a spectacular example of biological emergence. Despite detailed structural knowledge of individual BMC components, the predictive rules governing how these parts dynamically self-organize into functional mesoscale compartments across diverse bacterial species remain elusive. Understanding this emergence is critical for advancing synthetic biology and understanding microbial ecology. Our working group proposes a large-scale data synthesis project to decode the emergent assembly pathways of BMCs. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including comparative genomics, structural data, and proteomics from repositories such as the NCBI, the Protein Data Bank, and PRIDE. By leveraging advanced structural bioinformatics, AlphaFold-multimer predictions, and deep learning-based kinetic modeling, we will synthesize these datasets to predict BMC assembly pathways. This project relies entirely on existing data, using innovative AI strategies to map the complex network of interactions that drive mesoscale protein condensation and shell formation. The multifaceted nature of BMC biology requires a transdisciplinary approach that exceeds the capacity of any single lab, making NCEMS support critical. We will convene a diverse team of structural biologists, microbiologists, computational biophysicists, and machine learning engineers. Our working group is structured to promote collaborative partnerships across diverse geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages, ensuring a broad range of scientific perspectives. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this long-standing microbial mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in structural data integration, AI-driven modeling, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale protein organelles influences higher-order metabolic outcomes, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.
main_idea: This research investigates how individual protein components dynamically self organize into precise bacterial microcompartments to address unknown rules of assembly. The study employs artificial intelligence and kinetic modeling to synthesize disparate structural and multi omics data into a unified framework. This project provides a novel computational paradigm that reveals how transient molecular interactions drive the emergence of robust biological architectures.

title: Emergence of Lipid Homeostasis through Peroxisome Biogenesis Networks
title_norm: emergence of lipid homeostasis through peroxisome biogenesis networks
standardized_text:
This project investigates the mesoscale organization of peroxisomes and their role in lipid metabolism within cell biology. The molecular rules governing how protein import and lipid sorting determine the global abundance of peroxisome networks remain unknown. This study models the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis to explain how organelle architecture regulates cellular lipid homeostasis.

The study uses a data driven synthesis design to develop predictive computational models from existing public datasets. The team applies computer vision and graph neural networks alongside multi omics factor analysis to analyze the data. Machine learning models are validated by their ability to predict lipidomic profiles from spatial network metrics.

The project utilizes the Metabolomics Workbench and Image Data Resource plus BioGRID and STRING for protein interaction data. Semantic web technologies and biological ontologies integrate these distinct datasets into a single harmonized meta database. Automated curation pipelines mitigate data fragmentation and heterogeneity to ensure consistency across the integrated information sources.

The project spans a two year duration and includes four in person working group meetings for the team. The scope requires a convergence of expertise in cell biology and computational science to process large scale data.

All integrated datasets and analytical code will be published via Zenodo and GitHub for public access. The transdisciplinary team includes researchers across career stages and provides training opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows.

abstract_text: Peroxisomes are highly dynamic mesoscale organelles essential for cellular lipid metabolism and reactive oxygen species detoxification. Unlike mitochondria, peroxisomes can form de novo from the endoplasmic reticulum or multiply by fission, creating a highly adaptable, emergent metabolic network. The precise molecular rules governing how local protein import and membrane lipid sorting dictate the global abundance, size, and metabolic capacity of the peroxisomal compartment remain a major unresolved puzzle in cell biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is vital for deciphering how cells maintain lipid homeostasis under varying environmental stresses. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent properties of peroxisome biogenesis. We will systematically integrate publicly available lipidomics data, high-throughput fluorescence microscopy, and interactomic datasets from the Metabolomics Workbench, the Image Data Resource, and BioGRID. By employing advanced computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools powered by machine learning, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the peroxisome network. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale metabolic emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating spatial imaging with functional lipidomics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together cell biologists, lipid biochemists, computational data scientists, and systems biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, network models, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale organelle networks influences higher-order cellular metabolism, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.

abstract_text: The Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery is a highly conserved set of proteins that drive membrane remodeling and scission away from the cytoplasm. This machinery functions in diverse cellular processes, including multivesicular body biogenesis, viral budding, and cytokinesis. The sequential assembly of ESCRT components into mesoscale helical filaments that constrict and cleave membranes represents a profound example of biophysical emergence. However, the universal rules governing how local, nanoscale protein-lipid interactions translate into the generation of massive, mesoscale mechanical forces for membrane scission remain highly contested. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including cryo-electron microscopy structures, single-molecule biophysics data, and cellular imaging from repositories such as the Electron Microscopy Data Bank and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced molecular dynamics simulations guided by machine learning and topological data analysis, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the spatio-temporal dynamics of membrane constriction. This project relies entirely on existing public data, utilizing AI to extract novel insights into how local molecular interactions dictate the emergence of complex mesoscale forces. The integration of structural biophysics with cellular imaging requires a collaborative effort that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory, necessitating the support of NCEMS. We have assembled a diverse team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computer vision experts, and cellular ultrastructure specialists. Our working group is intentionally curated to include diverse scientific perspectives, bridging researchers from different institutional tiers and geographic locations. This collaborative environment will drive the innovative analytical strategies needed to solve this long-standing biological mystery. Furthermore, this project serves as a vital training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will gain hands-on experience in structural data integration, advanced image analysis, and open science practices. We are fully committed to making all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines freely available to the scientific community through open-source platforms like GitHub. By illuminating the relationship between protein assembly and membrane scission, this synthesis project will directly advance the NCEMS mission to understand the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.

This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary team spanning structural biology, biophysics, computational biology, and systems biology to synthesize publicly available data across multiple scales to decode the organizational logic of phase-separated condensates. We will integrate data from multiple public repositories including the Protein Data Bank (PDB), AlphaFold Database, PhaSePro, DrLLPS, STRING, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas. Third, we will construct multi-scale models linking molecular features to mesoscale organization and cellular function.

The project requires NCEMS support because it demands expertise spanning structural biology, bioinformatics, machine learning, biophysics, and cell biology that no single laboratory possesses. The data integration challenge alone requires computational infrastructure and expertise in harmonizing heterogeneous data types. Our team includes researchers from five institutions across three geographic regions, incorporating faculty at different career stages and from primarily undergraduate institutions.

We will host virtual workshops teaching data synthesis methods to the broader community. By synthesizing existing data at unprecedented scale, we will generate insights impossible for individual laboratories and establish frameworks for future synthesis research in cellular organization.

Protein interaction networks are not static entities but dynamically rewire across time, yet most network analyses treat interactions as fixed. This proposal addresses a fundamental gap: understanding how temporal dynamics of protein interactions give rise to emergent cellular behaviors. We hypothesize that time-dependent network rewiring follows predictable patterns that enable cells to transition between functional states, and that these patterns can be decoded through synthesis of existing temporal proteomics, interactomics, and transcriptomics datasets.

Our multidisciplinary team brings together network scientists, systems biologists, chronobiologists, and computational biologists from six institutions to synthesize publicly available temporal datasets spanning cell cycle progression, circadian rhythms, and stress responses. We will integrate data from PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, ArrayExpress, BioGRID, IntAct, and published time-series studies. This includes phosphoproteomics capturing signaling dynamics, protein abundance measurements, interaction mapping studies, and single-cell RNA sequencing time courses.

The project pursues three synergistic aims. First, we will construct temporal protein interaction networks by integrating time-resolved proteomics with static interaction data, developing computational methods to infer interaction dynamics from protein abundance and modification changes. Second, we will identify conserved network motifs and rewiring patterns across different temporal programs, testing whether cells employ common strategies for network reorganization. Third, we will develop predictive models linking network dynamics to emergent cellular phenotypes such as cell division, metabolic switching, and stress adaptation.

This synthesis project requires NCEMS support for several reasons. The data integration challenge spans multiple data types, organisms, and experimental conditions requiring diverse expertise. No single laboratory has the breadth of knowledge needed to interpret patterns across cell cycle biology, circadian biology, and stress biology. The computational infrastructure for analyzing dynamic networks at this scale exceeds typical laboratory resources.

Our team composition reflects NCEMS values: researchers from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators; faculty spanning assistant to full professor ranks; and strong representation of early-career researchers. Geographic diversity spans East Coast, Midwest, and West Coast institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a temporal protein interaction database with visualization tools, (2) software for inferring interaction dynamics from proteomics data, (3) a catalog of conserved network rewiring motifs, and (4) mechanistic models of temporal emergence. All resources will be publicly released with comprehensive documentation.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between laboratories, a summer workshop on temporal network analysis, and mentored research experiences for undergraduates from partner institutions. This project will establish foundational principles for understanding how molecular interaction dynamics give rise to emergent cellular behaviors across time.

This project establishes a novel database and predictive modeling suite that defines how molecular reorganization governs emergent biological phenotypes.

This proposal unites structural biologists, mitochondrial biologists, lipidomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of mitochondrial contact sites and their functional consequences.

Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs), mitochondria-lysosome contacts, and mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces each possess distinct protein compositions and functions, but comprehensive understanding of their architecture-function relationships is lacking. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography data from EMPIAR revealing contact site ultrastructure, proteomics data from proximity labeling studies, lipidomics datasets, calcium imaging data, and metabolomics measurements. We will map protein complexes to contact site architectures and identify organizational principles. Our second aim connects contact site composition to function by integrating proteomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data across cell types and conditions. Machine learning approaches will identify compositional signatures predicting functional outcomes. Our third aim examines how contact site dysfunction contributes to disease by linking architectural and compositional features to disease phenotypes.

This project exemplifies the need for NCEMS support. Understanding contact sites requires expertise spanning membrane biology, structural biology, metabolism, and computational modeling that no single laboratory encompasses. Data integration across imaging, proteomics, and metabolomics modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables synthesis impossible through traditional single-laboratory efforts.

This proposal assembles biophysicists, structural biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode how crowding shapes cellular organization and function at the mesoscale.

Macromolecular crowding affects protein folding, diffusion, interaction kinetics, and phase behavior, but these effects have been studied in isolation. We hypothesize that integrating diverse data types will reveal emergent organizational principles arising from crowding that cannot be understood from any single data source. Our synthesis will integrate protein abundance data from PaxDb and proteomics repositories, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, diffusion measurements from FRAP and single-molecule tracking studies, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas and subcellular fractionation studies.

Our first aim constructs a quantitative map of the cellular crowding landscape by integrating protein abundance, size, and localization data to estimate local crowding across subcellular compartments. This comprehensive synthesis will reveal principles connecting IDR sequence features to functional outcomes.

Our third aim links IDR properties to emergent cellular behaviors including condensate formation, signaling hub function, and transcriptional regulation.

abstract_text: The lack of motility makes plants highly vulnerable to environmental anomalies such as periods of extreme high temperature known as heat waves. Plants can search for better habitats by exploiting seed mobility, which relies on completing the life cycle and producing seeds. Formation of reproductive organs and seed development requires the production of cells through cell division. The last stage of cell division, cytokinesis, encompasses many key cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signaling. While cytokinesis is highly sensitive to heat stress in plants adapted to temperate climates, cytokinesis is more resilient in species adapted to tropical zones. However, how heat stress affects cytokinesis and the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness across different plant species remains unknown. This project aims to compare changes in cytokinetic components under heat stress in susceptible and hardy species to characterize differential responses of genetic circuits responsible for specific cellular events during cytokinesis. The long term goal is to harness this data for identifying the bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness. The experimental approach here will be systematic analysis of publicly available data from single-cell and whole-organ omics data collected under control and high-temperature conditions including transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics. Predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks will inform future experimental design for their functional characterization leading to better understanding of cellular adaptation mechanisms to heat stress. This knowledge may provide insight into evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to different climates and improve predictions for heat resiliency at the level of individual plants and populations.

title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
title_norm: synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
standardized_text:
This project investigates bacterial physiology and systems biology to define the organization and evolution of bacterial gene expression states. Current knowledge remains fragmented because existing data are limited to isolated experiments without a standardized method for harmonization. The study creates a comprehensive atlas of cell states to identify fundamental principles of bacterial behavior and evolution.

The study design employs a hierarchical approach that maps gene expression space across diverse bacterial species through clustering. Key methods include the InGEST pipeline for data harmonization and machine learning for dimensional reduction and state prediction. Results will be validated using synthetic mixtures of pure state datasets and existing single cell bacterial transcriptomic data.

Datasets will be sourced from public repositories including OKgeneExpDB and E coli Expression 2 and Ecomics and PRECISE. These datasets will be integrated by applying standardized filtering and normalization through the InGEST pipeline and ortholog mapping. Systematic variation from different technologies will be addressed by developing algorithms to detect and adjust for technical anomalies.

The project follows a two year timeline with year one focusing on pipeline development and year two on expansion. Multi lab collaboration is required to manage large scale data synthesis and leverage specialized computational expertise for machine learning.

The project will release the InGEST pipeline and the bacterial cell state atlas as open source containerized resources. The proposal does not address the composition of the research team or the specific training opportunities provided.

abstract_text: Bacterial cells have evolved to adapt their molecular composition to maximize growth and survival. Our current knowledge of bacterial cell states is fragmented. Researchers often only analyze data they generate themselves—usually for just one strain under a limited number of conditions—because it is difficult to harmonize omics datasets collected with different technologies in different labs. Our NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to create a first-of-its-kind atlas of bacterial cell states. To manageably scale data collection and analysis, we will build from examining model Escherichia coli strains in lab conditions, to adding wild E. coli strains in natural environments such as the human gut, to including diverse bacterial species with additional cell states. We expect to identify distinct foci corresponding to bacterial growth states and lifestyles (e.g., replicating, starving, motile, biofilm, spore, viable but nonculturable) by mapping the organization and occupancy of cell state space with dimensional reduction approaches. We will examine to what extent the gene expression signatures of different cell states and the relationships among them are conserved during bacterial evolution. Finally, we will use this framework to create a classifier that predicts the cell state composition of a bacterial population from metatranscriptomic data. By following open-science practices, we will make our pipelines and datasets reusable and maintainable by the research community. Our project may reveal new bacterial cell states and ways that we can non-genetically reprogram bacteria to prevent them from adopting lifestyles that damage the environment and cause disease.
main_idea: This research investigates whether bacterial gene expression manifests as discrete conserved states or a continuous spectrum across diverse microbial species. The study employs a hierarchical computational pipeline to harmonize heterogeneous transcriptomic datasets into a unified feature space for machine learning. This project provides a comprehensive atlas of bacterial cell states and a predictive classifier for analyzing complex microbial population compositions.

title: Energetic Origins of Connectivity within Protein Interaction Networks
title_norm: energetic origins of connectivity within protein interaction networks
standardized_text:
Systems biology and protein biophysics investigate how protein stability and disorder influence the architecture of protein protein interaction networks. Current knowledge identifies scale free network topologies but lacks understanding of how proteostasis and physical mechanisms generate these patterns. This project determines how molecular constraints dictate global network evolution to establish a biophysical foundation for modern network biology.

The study design integrates biophysical protein descriptors into network construction and uses evolutionary simulations to test topological constraints. Key methods include network centrality analysis and computational protein stability estimation alongside generative modeling and genetic algorithms for network trajectories. Results will be benchmarked against experimental proteolysis data and protein half life measurements and cellular abundance datasets for validation.

The project utilizes large scale interactome datasets for multiple species alongside Gene Expression Omnibus data and GO and WikiPathways databases. Interactome data will be mapped to protein level biophysical descriptors and contextualized using condition specific expression and chaperone annotations. Known experimental biases and prediction difficulties will be mitigated through robust thresholding and simulation based validation and multiple centrality metrics.

The project timeline includes network construction and centrality computation followed by stability annotation and development of evolutionary simulation models. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate disparate data types and theoretical frameworks across biophysics and structural informatics and modeling.

The proposal does not address plans for making findings and code and data publicly available. The team includes experts in protein biophysics and network biology and evolutionary modeling comprising staff scientists and trainees.

abstract_text: At least 10% of cellular proteins are intrinsically unstable and fold with marginal efficiency. In the cell, these proteins are preferentially engaged by chaperones and quality control proteins that refold or degrade them. Similarly, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) preferentially interact with specific partners that they require for folding and function. Such proteins must exhibit bias in the types of protein-protein interactions they form within the cell. We therefore hypothesize that the emergent scaling properties of protein interaction networks arise, in part, from the promiscuous interactions formed by unstable proteins and the obligate interactions formed by IDPs. To test this hypothesis, we will analyze existing large-scale interactome datasets to explore the context of unstable and disordered proteins within interaction networks. By extending this approach to evaluate how proteins with various conformational properties are distributed across several unicellular and multicellular networks, we aim to uncover generalizable insights into how protein biophysics shapes network architecture. Additionally, by mapping the centrality of proteins involved in various supramolecular organization regimes, we will identify topological niches associated with the occurrence of liquid-liquid phase separation and quinary structure. Finally, to determine the extent to which these biases constrain network evolution, we will utilize genetic algorithms to explore how changes in the stability of the proteome restrict the topologies that are accessible through evolution. Together, these investigations will provide insights into the role of protein stability and binding efficiency in the evolution of PPI networks and how this relates to the molecular mechanisms of evolution.
main_idea: This research investigates how intrinsic protein stability and disorder dictate the emergent topological features and evolutionary constraints of cellular networks. The study integrates biophysical protein descriptors into evolutionary simulations to model how molecular constraints shape the global architecture of interactomes. This work establishes a foundational framework linking protein biophysics to network biology, explaining how molecular properties drive complex system evolution.

title: Elucidating emergent structures in cellular RNA-protein interaction networks
title_norm: elucidating emergent structures in cellular rnaprotein interaction networks
standardized_text:

Current knowledge remains fragmented across diverse experimental techniques which prevents a unified understanding of mRNP composition and architecture. This project develops computational tools to integrate disparate datasets and predict emergent behaviors of mRNP structures and functions.

The study design utilizes a computational framework to normalize heterogeneous datasets for constructing cell specific mRNP maps. Methods include AlphaFold and FINCHES for protein domains alongside neural networks and Mpipi for molecular dynamics simulations. Results are validated against the beta actin mRNP benchmark and existing mass spectrometry and proximity labeling datasets.

The project utilizes public RNA protein interaction datasets and protein protein interaction databases including CD Code and RNA Granule. Datasets are integrated by identifying shared linked features that serve as anchors for normalization across different experimental modalities. Data noise is mitigated by assigning confidence scores to interactions based on signal to noise assessments from the benchmark.

The project spans a two year duration with intermediate milestones for tool development and database construction and biological findings. This scope requires a cross disciplinary approach combining expertise in RNA biology and machine learning and statistics and biophysics.

All developed tools and databases and findings will be released as open source resources for the scientific community. The team includes three collaborating labs with expertise in RNA biology and biophysics and data science and undergraduates.

abstract_text: Messenger RNA molecules are constantly bound by proteins that regulate all aspects of their function, including their processing, localization, translation, and degradation1. These mRNA-protein complexes (mRNPs) can also interact with each other and assemble into higher-order structures that play critical roles in cellular organization and response to environmental stimuli1-3. Despite their importance, we lack a comprehensive map of these cellular RNA-protein interaction networks at both the nano and micro scales. Years of efforts by researchers across the globe have yielded a large, but disjointed, collection of datasets that map different aspects of RNA-protein interactions. Currently, we lack tools to integrate these datasets, preventing their synthesis into a coherent and interpretable interaction map. Here, we propose to develop tools to combine disparate data types to build transcriptome-wide maps of mRNPs, and their higher-order interactions within cells. We will then apply these tools to gain insights into long-standing biological mysteries, including the impacts of synonymous mutations and cell-type specific effects of widely expressed RNAs.

The project employs a computational framework that integrates heterogeneous datasets by utilizing shared linked features as anchors for data normalization. This approach provides a novel predictive model for assessing RNA fate and condensate partitioning within specific cellular environments and contexts.

title: Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation
title_norm: oceans of disorder elucidating the role of disordered proteins in cellular adaptation
standardized_text:
Molecular biology investigates how intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) facilitate evolutionary adaptation within diverse marine organisms and extreme environments. Current knowledge confirms that IDRs undergo conformational changes under stimuli but lacks a systematic link between biophysical properties and adaptation. This project catalogs marine IDRs and simulates their dynamics to reveal universal principles of protein plasticity for biotechnological applications.

The study design integrates a comprehensive IDR catalog with coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning models. Researchers will apply structural prediction tools and deep learning algorithms to map the molecular mechanisms governing protein adaptation. Results will be validated through comparative analysis of predicted trajectories against existing metagenomic data and experimental biophysical measurements.

The project utilizes protein sequences from the Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0 and environmental metadata from the OceanDNA database. These datasets will be integrated by linking protein sequences with environmental variables like temperature and salinity and genomic context. Known limitations regarding physiological prediction bias will be mitigated by supplementing structural models with coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations.

The project follows a twenty four month timeline starting with catalog construction and concluding with predictive modeling and design. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration between metagenomics and protein biophysics to bridge the gap between sequence and function.

The team will release a database of marine IDRs and all predictive models and computational tools for public use. The multidisciplinary group includes experts in bioinformatics and protein biophysics and machine learning supported by NCEMS staff scientists.

abstract_text: Intrinsically disordered proteins and protein regions (collectively IDRs) are key regulators of environmental sensing, owing to their ability to undergo conformational changes in response to physicochemical fluctuations. Despite evidence from individual studies, a comprehensive understanding of IDR-driven adaptations across diverse environments remains elusive. The deep sea, characterized by extreme and variable conditions such as temperature, pressure, and salinity, offers a unique opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Over the past decade, large-scale ocean sampling expeditions using shotgun metagenomics have revolutionized our understanding of marine biodiversity, providing access to the genetic diversity of organisms, from microbes to fish, thriving in these extreme habitats. These datasets offer an unprecedented opportunity to explore how IDRs have evolved as molecular sensors to support survival across varied environmental conditions. Here, we will, for the same time, use these metagenomic datasets to systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors. Our multidisciplinary team, with expertise in metagenomics, protein biophysics, cell biology, and deep learning, will integrate bioinformatics, simulations, machine learning, and theoretical approaches to uncover sequence-level and functional adaptations of IDRs across marine environments. The outcomes of this research will produce a comprehensive map of IDR adaptations in marine systems, revealing their emergent properties as molecular sensors and actuators. In addition to advancing fundamental insights into stress adaptation and evolutionary biology, this work will inform biotechnological innovations, including engineering robust systems for extreme environments.

The study integrates large scale metagenomic data with coarse grained molecular dynamics simulations to map protein conformational changes across environmental gradients. This work establishes a predictive framework for protein plasticity that enables the de novo design of resilient proteins for biotechnology.

abstract_text: Large-scale consortia like the Dependency Map and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia have generated extensive multi-omics data for over 2000 primary cell lines, including bulk measurements of DNA, chromatin accessibility, RNA, and proteins. Recently, multi-omics single-cell sequencing and imaging data labeling RNA and proteins for these cell lines have become increasingly available. However, these datasets remain fragmented, lacking integration into a unified framework to model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell. While previous efforts have created multimodal benchmark datasets, these often include diverse samples from multiple donors and heterogeneous cell types. In contrast, our project focuses on single model systems, such as commonly used cell lines, which already feature extensive single-cell, bulk sequencing, and imaging data. By eliminating donor and cell type variability, our approach enables robust analyses and precise alignment across modalities, including RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility. This focus on homogenous cell types within a consistent biological context facilitates mechanistic studies of regulatory interactions and perturbation responses, minimizing confounding variability. We aim to develop multimodal frameworks for 7 cell lines and computational pipelines to analyze relationships across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. By incorporating additional multi-omics data, including bulk and single-cell perturbation datasets (e.g., loss-of-function screens and Perturb-seq), we will create a comprehensive benchmarking resource. With expertise in machine learning, network biology, and genomics, and NCEMS support for data wrangling, our team will deliver tools to study regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. These efforts will foster fundamental discoveries, community-driven resource development, and innovation in multi-omics research.
main_idea: Current research lacks a unified framework to integrate fragmented DNA, RNA, and protein data within individual human cell line models. This proposal employs machine learning and network biology to align bulk and single cell datasets across consistent biological regulatory contexts. The project establishes a comprehensive benchmarking resource that enables precise mechanistic study of regulatory interactions through integrated multi omics analysis.

title: From image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
title_norm: from image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning
standardized_text:

Current knowledge contains vast morphological and proteomic data that remain siloed and prevent a comprehensive systems level analysis. This project develops a computational framework to predict cellular architecture and shifts the focus toward physical and geometric principles.

The study design employs a two step strategy to align multicomponent image data and infer predictive relationships between features. The methodology utilizes Gromov Wasserstein distance analysis and transfer learning alongside generative adversarial networks and agent based modeling. Results are validated by benchmarking predictions against complete datasets and using in vitro and in silico data as baselines.

The research utilizes existing cell imaging data and in vitro reconstitution data alongside published molecular simulation outcomes for analysis. Distinct data spaces are integrated through Gromov Wasserstein distances to generate similarity matrices for the synthesis of feature sets. Known limitations regarding data availability and quality are mitigated through systematic literature synthesis and rigorous data curation efforts.

The project spans two years with an initial phase for workflow development followed by expansion to complex three component systems. This scope requires a multi lab approach to combine expertise in computational image analysis and mathematical modeling and biophysics.

The project produces an open source data integration workflow and contributes curated datasets to the broader scientific research community. The proposal does not address the specific composition of the team beyond noting the involvement of various field leaders.

abstract_text: Mesoscale cellular organization emerges from complex interactions among chemical, structural, and physical components. Understanding how mesoscale structures influence local and collective cellular properties remains a significant challenge, often beyond the scope of individual experimental studies. While vast image datasets for cellular components exist, their full potential for deeper secondary analysis and synthesis remains untapped. We propose to synthesize morphological and physico-chemical measurements from cell image, in vitro, and in silico data to unravel the principles of mesoscale cellular organization. Our approach will develop a pipeline using transfer learning and mutual prediction, trained on complete datasets (all components of interest present) and applied to incomplete datasets (missing one or more components). This methodology will uncover relationships between cellular components and enable holistic systems-level predictions. To demonstrate the generalizability and biological relevance of this approach, we will test it on three increasingly complex mesoscale systems centered on the nucleus: (1) nucleus-nucleolus, (2) nucleus-centrosome-microtubules, and (3) nucleus-mitochondria-mitochondrial condensates. These test cases will showcase how our method integrates and predicts complex systems relationships, advancing our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization.

title: Transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation
title_norm: transposable elements and the emergence of genomic innovation

abstract_text: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a powerful structural proteomics method that can provide high-resolution structural information about complex mixtures of proteins in their native physiological context.1,2,3 The method works by chemically crosslinking two reactive amino acid residues that are close to one another in 3-D space, thereby freezing this spatial information into a covalent bond, and then retrieving this information by sequencing crosslinked peptides following enzymatic digest of the constituent proteins (like Hi-C,4 but for proteins). Initially developed in the 2000s to interrogate purified proteins, by the late-2010s, methods became available to interrogate protein-protein interactions (PPIs) on the proteome-scale and in the cellular environment.5 This project seeks to standardize, combine, and integrate existing publicly available crosslinking datasets from PRIDE to make these data more re-usable and useful for integrative and hybrid modeling. We will also create a meta-dataset to catalogue PPIs in human and other model organisms. Because XL-MS encodes information about both protein identity and interacting residues, these findings can be cross-validated to structural predictions of protein complexes using AlphaFold3, thereby providing stronger evidence for their existence compared to huMAP3.0, which predicts protein complexes without structural evidence. We will integrate these findings into the EBI Complex Portal to make it accessible to the life science community.
main_idea: Fragmented crosslinking mass spectrometry data currently lack the standardized processing and metadata required to validate complex protein interaction network models. This proposal employs uniform reprocessing of legacy datasets using modern search algorithms to enable rigorous structural verification against predictive models. The project establishes a unified repository of validated residue level interactions that bridges the gap between experimental proteomics and structural biology.

By leveraging structured data standards, metadata will be enriched with controlled vocabulary terms, enhancing dataset transparency and usability. title: Emergent Order Parameters of Allostery: An AI Framework for Predicting and Engineering Protein Regulation
title_norm: emergent order parameters of allostery an ai framework for predicting and engineering protein regulation
standardized_text:
The field of protein biophysics lacks a predictive framework to classify allosteric regulation across diverse protein systems. Current models focus on discrete structural transitions while modern network methods lack grounding in physical energetic coupling. This project develops a physics informed data science framework to quantify allosteric communication for rational drug design.

The study integrates molecular dynamics simulations and deep mutational scanning data to derive dynamic descriptors for protein classification. The approach utilizes time dependent linear response models and nonlinear dimensionality reduction alongside machine learning for predictive modeling. Results are validated through experimental testing of designed mutations in transcription factors using biophysical assays of binding affinity.

The project utilizes datasets from MaveDB and MDRepo alongside evolutionary sequence databases to inform the computational analysis. These distinct datasets are integrated by mapping dynamic coupling metrics and functional fitness scores into a unified coordinate system. Incomplete molecular dynamics data are mitigated by generating structural models via BioEmu and performing new simulations on Folding@home.

The project spans twenty four months with distinct phases for data integration and descriptor development and experimental validation. The scope requires collaboration between experts in dynamics modeling and large scale machine learning and experimental transcription factor biology.

The team will release open source analytical tools and curated datasets to the public to ensure research transparency. The interdisciplinary team includes biophysicists and computational scientists and experimentalists across various career stages including staff scientists and assistants.

abstract_text: Allostery—the ability of a perturbation at one site in a protein to control function at a distant site— underlies enzyme catalysis, signaling, and gene regulation. Yet we still lack a general, quantitative way to define how “allosteric” a protein is, to compare that across systems, and to predict how substitutions will strengthen, weaken, or rewire that control. This project develops a physics-informed data science framework to obtain quantitative order parameters of allostery and use them to classify, predict, and ultimately engineer regulatory behavior. We will integrate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets, and evolutionary information (Table 1) to extract dynamic coupling measures that report how a local perturbation propagates through the protein over time. From these data we will derive physically interpretable allosteric order parameters that quantify three key features: (i) strength of long-range communication, (ii) directionality/asymmetry of information flow, and (iii) timescale of propagation. These parameters will form the basis of an “allostery score” that allows us to categorize the degree and mode of allostery across proteins and across species. We will then train machine learning models to predict how specific amino acid substitutions alter these order parameters — i.e., how a mutation changes not just local stability, but global regulatory wiring. Finally, we will apply this framework to design mutations that reprogram allosteric regulation in transcription factors, and experimentally test these designs. The outcome is a generalizable, predictive map from sequence to allosteric control.
main_idea: This research addresses the absence of a predictive framework for quantifying allosteric regulation across diverse protein systems by integrating dynamics. The study employs a physics informed data science approach that maps molecular simulations and evolutionary patterns into unified coordinate systems. This project establishes a universal theory of allostery to enable the rational design of synthetic regulatory proteins and drugs.

abstract_text: Proteins can adopt intricate three-dimensional structures, including complex topologies such as knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, and even more complex structures. These entangled architectures challenge traditional views of protein folding and stability, suggesting that nature may use topological complexity as a mechanism to fine-tune function, regulation, or mechanical resilience. Despite growing structural data, the evolutionary origins and functional consequences of these nontrivial topologies remain largely unexplored. This project aims to leverage existing databases to identify the evolutionary turning points at which topological changes first arose within protein families. By integrating sequence, structural, and phylogenetic data from resources such as UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold, AlphaKnot, and AlphaLasso, we will reconstruct annotated phylogenetic trees that map the emergence and diversification of entangled proteins across evolutionary time. We will analyze whether specific sequence motifs, disulfide patterns, or intrinsically disordered regions are associated with the onset of entanglement, and whether such proteins are enriched in pathogenic or stress-adapted organisms. Furthermore, we will assess how topological complexity correlates with functional hotspots, including catalytic or allosteric regions, to reveal possible adaptive advantages. This work will establish a framework to trace, predict, and design protein topologies with distinct structural and functional characteristics. The outcomes will not only deepen our understanding of how topology shapes evolution and biomolecular behavior but also provide an open, data-driven platform for studying entanglement as a functional and evolutionary principle in protein science.

The study employs a comparative evolutionary analysis that integrates phylogenetic reconstruction with structural bioinformatics to map topological changes across diverse protein families. title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
title_norm: deciphering systemic biological networks through aidriven multiomic integration
standardized_text:

Current knowledge documents single organ responses but lacks integrated networks due to the use of heterogeneous and non-homologous datasets. This project maps molecular networks and builds a digital twin rat model to provide dynamic insights into systemic function.

The study design integrates multi-omic data vertically within organs and horizontally across organs using a reaction diffusion graph network. Methods include principal component analysis and physics informed neural networks to model nonlinear biochemical processes and identify key regulatory nodes. Results are validated by comparing model predictions against empirical data through cross validation and sensitivity analyses of the system.

The study utilizes the MoTrPAC dataset which contains multi-omic data from eighteen rat tissues to analyze systemic physiological adaptation. Datasets are synthesized by mapping molecular responses across time using a graph Laplacian operator and a neural network model. Inconsistencies in data structure are mitigated through standardized preprocessing and the application of a hybrid mechanistic and data driven framework.

Year one milestones include proof of principle integration and grant submission while year two focuses on mapping inter-organ interactions. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because the lead lacks the computational and AI expertise to integrate large scale datasets.

The proposal does not address plans for making findings or code publicly available. The team requires expertise in biology and computational data science but specific career stages are not detailed here.

abstract_text: Organ cross-talk refers to the bidirectional communication between different organs that enables the body to maintain physiological homeostasis, respond and adapt during dynamic states. Disturbances to these inter-organ communication networks may result in inappropriate physiological responses, thereby compromising systemic function. This proposal will leverage a unique publicly available large-scale, multi-organ, multi-omic dataset comprising 18 solid tissues from rats subjected to an endurance exercise training program. Our hypothesis is that organ-specific signaling hierarchies will determines the coordinated multiorgan responses that drive systemic adaptation. Following organ-specific multi-omic vertical integration, we will determine 1) the predictors of phenotypic adaptations, and 2) the cross talk between organs via horizontal integration. The computed networks will provide the foundation to generate a digital twin rat which will serve as a valuable tool to model organismal responses to physiological, environmental and pharmacological challenges. This comprehensive, temporally resolved analysis will offer unprecedented insights into how molecular interactions are coordinated across organs and levels of organization to determine whole-organism physiological function.

The study employs a reaction diffusion graph network integrated with physics informed neural networks to model nonlinear biochemical signaling processes dynamically. abstract_text: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins play essential roles in regulation, signaling, and molecular recognition, yet their evolutionary conservation patterns remain poorly understood. While folded domains exhibit clear conservation of structure and function, IDRs evolve rapidly and appear sequence diverse, obscuring how they encode functional specificity. Bridging the sequence function relationship in IDRs and even their reliable functional annotation remains a major challenge. Emerging evidence, however, suggests that subsets of IDRs harbor conserved sequence features such as short linear motifs (SLiMs), charge patterning and aromatic clustering that give rise to transient structural elements and encode critical molecular functions. This project aims to systematically identify and characterize the most conserved IDRs across proteomes by integrating large-scale sequence alignments, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and experimental functional annotations from publicly available databases. By combining resources such as UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif (ELM), IDRome, and MaveDB, we will quantify the interplay between evolutionary, structural, and functional signatures of conservation in disordered regions. Our multidisciplinary Working Group unites computational and experimental biophysics to build a curated, open-access database of conserved IDRs. This synthesis effort will reveal how dynamic, flexible protein regions maintain specific and evolvable functions, an emergent property at the mesoscale interface between sequence evolution, molecular structure, and cellular regulation.

The study employs a multi scale integrative approach that combines molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning to analyze evolutionary conservation. title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation

The project commits to open science by releasing open source software and a curated dataset of hibernation studies. The team includes specialists in cell physiology and genomics and bioinformatics who provide training opportunities for staff scientists.

abstract_text: Hibernation is a complex physiological strategy that allows certain mammals to withstand prolonged periods of resource scarcity and low temperatures by dramatically suppressing metabolism, while maintaining organ integrity and preserving muscle and bone mass. Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.
main_idea: This research investigates the molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation by addressing the lack of comparative frameworks for analyzing transcriptional variation. The study employs phylogenetic models of gene expression evolution to distinguish conserved regulatory processes from lineage specific adaptations across diverse species. This work provides a novel computational resource that identifies core genes enabling metabolic suppression and tissue protection in hibernating mammals.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
standardized_text:
This project investigates protein biophysics and molecular evolution to address the lack of negative examples in allosteric databases. Current knowledge recognizes allostery as a regulatory mechanism but fails to distinguish allosteric proteins from non allosteric homologs. The study identifies biophysical determinants of allostery to enable the annotation of new systems and the design of synthetic proteins.

The study design involves creating a curated allosterome database followed by computational analysis of allosteric and non allosteric homologs. The team applies Adaptive Steered Molecular Dynamics and Statistical Coupling Analysis alongside machine learning classification to identify key protein features. Results are validated by the ability of models to predict allosteric status and propose mutations that modulate protein activity.

The project utilizes the Allosteric Database and the Transport Protein Data Base alongside MAVEdb and InterPro and UniProt and PDB. Datasets are integrated by labeling transporter protein families based on evidence of allosteric regulation using domain insertion as a proxy. Sparse data and inconsistent formatting are mitigated by curating a balanced dataset of allosteric and non allosteric protein entries.

The project spans twenty four months and includes phases for dataset curation and analysis and model generation and manuscript preparation. The scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise in machine learning and protein biophysics and molecular evolution and experimental biochemistry.

The augmented allosterome database and research findings will be made available to the community through the CyVerse platform and publications. The team includes experts in materials chemistry and chemical physics and machine learning and computational biophysics and experimental biophysics and evolution.

abstract_text: Allostery is a fundamental property of proteins wherein perturbations at one site can influence another distant site. Understanding the sequence, structural, and dynamic determinants of allostery is critical to engineering new biosensors, designing allosteric modulators, and predicting the functional impact of mutations. For many proteins, allostery allows control of protein activity in response to external stimuli, such as ligand binding, protein or nucleic acid interactions, post-translational modifications, light, and redox state. There are proteins, though, that do not clearly exhibit such regulatory mechanisms, and are thus rarely included in publicly available allosteric databases. Consequently, it remains unclear what features distinguish regulated systems and regulatory sites from their non-regulated counterparts. To this end, we will focus our work on a specific class of proteins—namely transporter proteins—and assemble a database that is, on the one hand, very specific—restricted to all such proteins, and broad because it includes proteins for which there is a lack of evidence for allosteric regulation. This augmented allosteric database will provide a basis for identifying the degree of allostery in proteins. Through these databases, and associated computational interrogations, we will reveal the determinants of allostery in transporter proteins, a large and diverse family of membrane proteins comprised of allosteric and non-allosteric members.
main_idea: This research investigates the biophysical determinants of allostery in transporter proteins to resolve why current databases lack essential negative controls. The study employs a comparative analysis of allosteric and non-allosteric homologs using integrated machine learning models and molecular dynamics simulations. This work provides a comprehensive framework for predicting allosteric regulation and enables the rational design of synthetic systems for protein control.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
standardized_text:
Evolutionary systems biology investigates molecular organization at the mesoscale level to address gaps in current evolutionary synthesis frameworks. Existing models analyze genomic and multi-omics data in isolation without grounding population genetic variation in mechanistic biochemistry. This project develops a machine learning synthesis framework to identify conserved mesoscale modules that reveal fundamental evolutionary design principles.

The study design involves data harmonization and hybrid machine learning models to identify shared and lineage specific molecular modules. The team applies graph neural networks and genome scale metabolic modeling to infer regulatory networks and metabolic constraints. Results are validated through flux balance analysis and alignment metrics to ensure module reproducibility and high predictive accuracy.

The project utilizes human datasets from GTEx and All of Us alongside mosquito data from Ag1000G and VectorBase. Distinct datasets are integrated through standardized ontologies and orthology mappings to create unified pathway scaffolds for comparative analysis. Potential data sparsity in mosquito variants is mitigated by prioritizing curated subsets and applying transfer learning for alignment.

The two year timeline includes phases for data harmonization and model training followed by manifold alignment and final release. The project requires cross disciplinary collaboration between machine learning and population genetics experts to integrate disparate data and models.

All workflows and models are FAIR compliant and archived with digital object identifiers to ensure public access and reuse. The team includes experts in machine learning and metabolic modeling supported by staff scientists for workflow deployment and curation.

abstract_text: Living systems exhibit emergent organization that bridges molecular and evolutionary scales. Genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic dynamics interact across levels of complexity to produce coordinated cellular behavior, yet most datasets capture only one layer at a time. Despite vast genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic resources across species and environments, no synthesis framework connects these data to reveal how evolutionary forces shape the mesoscale—the intermediate level where genes, proteins, and metabolites assemble into adaptive networks. The SynEvo Working Group will develop a machine-learning–driven synthesis framework that unites population-genetic and multi-omics data to uncover conserved and divergent axes of molecular organization. Using well-characterized human and mosquito datasets, we will identify how genetic variation, regulatory control, and metabolic flux interact to produce conserved mesoscale modules reflecting evolutionary constraint and innovation. These contrasting systems serve as testbeds for uncovering evolutionary design principles of molecular coordination—how selection and constraint shape regulatory–metabolic organization across life. SynEvo integrates interpretable machine learning with genome-scale metabolic (GEM) and MiReN (Minimal Regulatory Network; MILP-based regulatory inference) approaches, producing an open SynEvo Atlas hosted within NCEMS infrastructure—a reusable resource for evolutionary systems biology. By revealing both species- specific adaptations and conserved mesoscale design principles, SynEvo will advance conceptual and computational frontiers, providing fundamental insight into how life organizes itself across molecular, physiological, and evolutionary dimensions, with applications to human health, malaria transmission, and environmental resilience.
main_idea: This research addresses the lack of a synthesis framework connecting population genetic variation with multi omics data to explain mesoscale molecular organization. The study employs hybrid machine learning models and manifold alignment to integrate disparate biological datasets into a unified and mechanistically constrained representation. This project creates a novel atlas that reveals evolutionary design principles by identifying conserved and divergent molecular modules across diverse species.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
standardized_text:
Cellular biology investigates protein turnover kinetics to address the lack of a unified framework for determining protein stability. Current knowledge of protein degradation remains fragmented across heterogeneous datasets that prevent comprehensive meta analysis or cross kingdom comparisons. This project harmonizes proteome turnover data to identify evolutionary principles of protein stability and establish standardized reporting practices.

The study design involves systematic assembly and integration of protein half life datasets using a unified computational workflow. Methods include kinetic modeling and machine learning (deep neural networks) alongside ortholog mapping and multivariate regression analysis. Results will be validated through Bayesian sampling and comparison of prediction accuracy against existing baseline degron databases.

Datasets are sourced from public repositories including PRIDE for organisms such as E. coli and H. sapiens. Integration occurs by refitting turnover rates with consistent kinetic models and mapping orthologs via OrthoDB and UniProt. Variations in labeling strategies are mitigated by correcting for precursor enrichment kinetics and applying unified normalization procedures.

The project follows a 24 month timeline starting with data cataloging and ending with public release of tools. Multi lab collaboration combines expertise in proteomics and systems biology to ensure rigorous data harmonization and synthesis.

All data and analysis pipelines will be released through CyVerse and GitHub while adhering to FAIR principles. The team includes principal investigators and staff scientists with expertise in mass spectrometry and data integration.
