abstract_text: Proteins vary widely in how long they persist within cells, from minutes to years, and this variation plays a central role in regulating biological function and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Decades of research have revealed several mechanisms that influence protein half-lives across the kingdoms of life. However, the differential impact of these mechanisms on protein half-lives within and between species remains incompletely understood. This knowledge gap can be addressed by comprehensive analyses of global proteome stability datasets enabled by recent advances in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. However, these datasets are currently fragmented across heterogeneous studies that are not easily amenable to meta-analysis. This Working Group will bring together complementary expertise in proteomics, computational biology, systems biochemistry, and evolution to systematically harmonize and integrate publicly available datasets on protein turnover across four representative species across two kingdoms of life - E. coli, S. cerevisiae, M. musculus, and H. sapiens. By reanalyzing existing data using consistent approaches and unifying metadata standards, we will generate a comprehensive, comparable, and publicly accessible resource, the Protein Stability Database (PSD). This database will enable us to identify the molecular and evolutionary principles that govern protein stability and assess how turnover patterns vary across different cell types and organisms. Beyond addressing these core questions, our Working Group aims to establish best practices and a shared vocabulary for measuring and reporting protein turnover, enabling seamless incorporation of future datasets and integration with other NCEMS data resources.
main_idea: This research addresses the lack of a unified framework for understanding protein turnover kinetics and stability across diverse biological species. The study employs a standardized computational workflow to integrate fragmented proteomic datasets through kinetic modeling and deep learning protein embeddings. This project establishes the first cross kingdom comparison of protein homeostasis to reveal fundamental evolutionary principles governing cellular protein stability.

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
standardized_text:
Spatial omics integrates high plex RNA and protein imaging to characterize cell states within complex biological tissue environments. Current methods treat transcriptomics and proteomics as separate abundance snapshots while lacking subcellular resolution for spatial organization analysis. This project develops a predictive synthesis framework to define biophysical cell states and forecast cell fate using spatial organization.

The study employs a three step computational pipeline to register images and harmonize data onto a shared grid. The approach utilizes STalign and SEraster tools alongside contrastive multimodal embedding and deep learning vision foundation models like SubCell. Results are validated against abundance only baselines using registration metrics and cross modal predictive accuracy with spatial shuffles.

The research utilizes the Spatch validation set and curated public cohorts to address the primary research question. Distinct datasets are integrated by registering adjacent sections into a common coordinate frame and aggregating molecular expression data. Non rigid imaging distortions are mitigated through LDDMM alignment while data heterogeneity is addressed using NCEMS supported harmonization.

The project follows a twenty four month timeline divided into eight quarters covering development and final dissemination phases. The scope requires expertise in machine learning and biophysics and statistical physics and cell biology across multiple laboratories.

All code and trained models and harmonized datasets will be released under permissive licenses with containerized reproducible workflows. The team includes principal investigators across four disciplines supported by NCEMS staff scientists specializing in bioinformatics and cloud deployment.

abstract_text: Cell states reflect not only molecular abundance but also where molecules reside. Public spatial omics (Spatch) now provide high-plex RNA (Xenium/CosMx) and protein (CODEX) maps, yet cross-modal synthesis at subcellular scales remain fragmented. We will develop an open, end-to-end synthesis framework that (i) registers adjacent-section spatial RNA-Protein images at subcellular resolution using diffeomorphic alignment (STalign), (ii) harmonizes RNA features into protein-scale rasters (SEraster) to create a one-to-one correspondence of patches to be compared (iii) quantify membrane/nuclear proximity, polarity, local density, and other features (iv) trains RNA-to-protein predictors and learn a unified biophysical fingerprint of cell state. Using the paired Xenium/CosMx-CODEX cancer atlas as a validation set and curated public cohorts as application sets, we will benchmark against abundance-only baselines. Framework performance will be assessed by overall registration quality, verified patch correspondence, and cross-modal predictive accuracy, with appropriate positive and negative controls to rule out leakage and spurious structure. We will test the hypotheses that RNA-protein spatial relationships yield predictive signals for cell state beyond abundance and that low- dimensional biophysical fingerprints precede and predict cell fate decisions. All code, trained models, and harmonized datasets generated from this work will be released under permissive licenses with containerized, reproducible workflows and scheduled public snapshots. This community-scale synthesis will convert dispersed spatial imaging datasets into predictive, interpretable models of cell state, while leveraging NCEMS (CyVerse compute, data harmonization, and project management) for scalable analysis and dissemination.
main_idea: This research addresses the inability of current spatial omics to synthesize RNA and protein data at subcellular resolution for analysis. The project employs a computational pipeline that harmonizes cross modal imaging onto shared pixel grids to quantify complex biophysical features. This framework provides a novel predictive model that uses subcellular organization to forecast cell fate beyond simple molecular abundance.

title: Integrating AI and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Quantitative Prediction of Enzyme Functions
title_norm: integrating ai and molecular dynamics simulations for quantitative prediction of enzyme functions
standardized_text:
Biomolecular research studies enzyme function prediction using artificial intelligence and molecular dynamics to address current gaps in structural modeling. Current models provide accurate static predictions but lack the temporal and mechanistic information captured by molecular dynamics simulations. This project integrates multi scale simulation data into a multi modal framework to improve predictive accuracy for therapeutic design.

The study design involves comprehensive data curation followed by the synthesis of information into a multi modal model. The framework utilizes spatio temporal graph neural networks and gated fusion modules alongside all atom and coarse grained simulations. Results are validated by benchmarking against existing sequence and structure based models using Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission metrics.

The project utilizes datasets from UniProt SwissProt and PDB alongside simulation derived data from ATLAS and md CATH repositories. Multi modal learning techniques fuse sequence and structural embeddings with multi resolution dynamic embeddings into a single unified representation. Limited conformational sampling is mitigated by using enhanced sampling techniques and validation across multiple force fields for all simulations.

The project spans twenty four months with twelve months dedicated to data curation and twelve months for model benchmarking. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in biophysical analysis and AI development with large scale computational resources.

All processed trajectories and code will be deposited in open repositories and findings will appear in open access journals. The team includes experts in simulation and bioinformatics across various career stages supported by staff scientists and research assistants.

abstract_text: Recent AI advances have transformed biomolecular research, enabling accurate prediction of biomolecu- lar functions from sequence and structural data. However, the role of dynamic motions and environmental responses in shaping biomolecular function remains underexplored in AI-driven approaches. In this pro- posal, our working group aims to bridge this gap by integrating temporal and physicochemical insights from molecular dynamics (MD) with AI techniques to enhance predictive accuracy in protein function, focusing on enzymes. We will work closely with NCEMS in two phases: (I) Comprehensive data curation of enzyme function annotations, collection of multi-scale simulation trajectories, and biophysical deter- minants causally linked to enzyme activity. (II) Synthesizing simulations and biophysical determinants through a multi-modal AI model to enhance enzyme function predictions. The project integrates comple- mentary expertise across multiple labs and will leverage NCEMS computational resources to generate large-scale data. By synergizing AI and MD, we will advance biomolecular modeling beyond the static sequence-structure paradigm to include temporal resolution, guiding rational design of therapeutic and functional biomolecules.
main_idea: Current enzyme function prediction models fail because they rely on static structural data rather than essential temporal protein dynamics. This proposal integrates multi scale molecular dynamics simulations into a multi modal artificial intelligence framework using spatio temporal graph networks. The resulting model provides a novel predictive architecture that captures protein motion to improve the accuracy of functional annotations.

title: Discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
title_norm: discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
standardized_text:
Bacterial cell biology investigates the distribution and function of organelles within complex microbial communities to address current knowledge gaps. While molecular mechanisms exist for model systems, the regulatory dynamics of these organelles in natural microbiomes remain uncharacterized. This study maps the diversity of bacterial organelles in the human gut to shift research toward complex ecological contexts.

The study employs a community synthesis approach to categorize organelle expression patterns across diverse metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets. Researchers will apply Hidden Markov Models and machine learning models alongside gene neighborhood analysis to identify and characterize these structures. Results will be validated by cross referencing metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic data and benchmarking against curated metagenomic datasets.

The project utilizes human gut metagenomes from the GMrepo database and the IBD Multi omics Database for analysis. These distinct datasets will be integrated to correlate organelle presence with functional expression and specific environmental conditions. Potential false positives in identifying encapsulins will be mitigated by refining model thresholds and using multi omics validation.

The project spans two years from February 2026 to January 2028 including phases for pipeline development and data processing. This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to integrate expertise across organelle classes and leverage infrastructure for large scale data harmonization.

The team will create a publicly accessible database of bacterial organelles and publish findings in peer reviewed journals. The multi disciplinary team includes experts in bacterial genetics and computational biology alongside early career researchers and staff scientists.

abstract_text: Once considered exclusive to eukaryotes, subcellular organelles are now recognized as common features of prokaryotic cells. Bacterial organelles exhibit remarkable diversity and specialization, falling into three structural classes: protein-bounded compart- ments, lipid-bounded compartments, and biomolecular condensates. While recent model sys- tem studies have uncovered molecular mechanisms controlling the formation and function of several bacterial organelles, their activities in ecological contexts, environmental responsive- ness, and inter-organelle interactions remain poorly characterized. Here, we propose a com- munity synthesis approach to define the landscape of bacterial organelles in the human gut mi- crobiome using publicly available multi-omics data. We have assembled a team of experts on the genetics and biochemistry of bacterial microcompartments, encapsulins, ferrosomes, and biomolecular condensates. With input from NCEMS staff we will enumerate the occurrence of bacterial organelles from metagenomic datasets and examine meta-transcriptomic and meta- proteomic data to characterize their regulation and expression. This framework will allow us to test key hypotheses, such as whether organelles with overlapping functions can co-exist within the same organisms as well as various members of a microbial community and how organelle expression patterns change in response to environmental conditions. We will also examine co- ordinated expression between organelles, which will provide insights into potential inter-orga- nelle interactions. These studies will form the basis for publications on the distribution, co-oc- currence, and functional roles of bacterial organelles. The generated data will guide future hy- potheses, shed light on the evolutionary trajectory of cellular compartmentalization, and enable the rational design of biotechnological applications based on the unique features of bacterial organelles.
main_idea: This research addresses the unknown regulatory dynamics and ecological distribution of bacterial organelles within complex human gut microbial communities today. The study employs a community synthesis approach by integrating multi omics datasets through machine learning models and co expression network analysis. This project establishes the first comprehensive database of bacterial organelle expression patterns to reveal evolutionary trends across diverse microbiomes.
